NFL Play-by-Play · 2000–2025 · every snap

Everybody knows.
The data doesn't.

Five things the whole sport repeats — the run sets up the pass, ice the kicker, keep the defense guessing — measured against a quarter-century of every play ever charted. They don't hold up.

532k+ plays modeled 26 seasons 5 myths on trial
Scroll to the first snap
01Offense

“You've got to establish the run to set up the pass.”

Verdict — myth

Line up every pass in the league and ask a simple question: does it gain more when the previous play was a run? It doesn't.

On 1st-and-10, a called pass after a run is worth 0.015 expected points fewer than a pass after a pass — a difference statistically indistinguishable from zero. Check every game state — short yardage, red zone, 2nd-and-long — and every one lands inside the "no effect" band. Running first doesn't soften the defense for the throw. It just uses up a down.

02Play-calling

“The great play-callers keep a defense guessing.”

Verdict — backwards

It's the opposite. Once you account for situation, the most predictable play-callers run the best offenses.

Raw numbers say unpredictable teams score more — but that's a mirage: good offenses simply live in friendlier down-and-distance, where the run/pass split is naturally balanced. Compare each caller to the league in the exact same situations and the sign flips. And the poster child is the man the booth mocks for it: Andy Reid is the easiest elite play-caller to predict — and runs the single best offense in football.

03Special teams

“Call timeout — freeze him — ice the kicker.”

Verdict — can't tell it from luck

Twenty-six seasons and 2,221 pressure kicks later, icing shaves maybe three points off a make — but the effect can't be told apart from doing nothing at all.

Control for distance, kicker quality, weather and the moment, and icing is worth −2.9 points of make probability with a confidence interval that runs straight through zero. Score every coach's personal icing record against luck and 20 of 21 fall inside the noise cone. The one that pokes out — Pete Carroll — is exactly the single fluke you'd expect from 21 tries. Nobody owns the ice.

04Game management

The two ways a coach wastes a timeout — and who does it most.

Verdict — names named

A timeout gets wasted two ways: burned early to escape a play-clock jam, or hoarded until it dies unused in a one-score loss. Different coaches, different sins.

Mike Martz burned them at twice the league rate in every season he coached. Norv Turner let a timeout die in his pocket in 35% of his close losses — the league does it 15% of the time. And the twist the booth never mentions: Andy Reid, endlessly roasted for clock management, almost never dies with timeouts unused — 4 times in 61 close losses, the best rate of any long-tenured coach.

05Defense · the closer

“Whatever you do, don't take the pass-interference penalty.”

Verdict — sometimes the smart play

On a deep ball, grabbing the receiver and eating the flag costs the defense less than letting him catch it. The penalty moves the ball the same distance — but erases the yards after the catch and the touchdown.

Here's the gamble, though. The foul is a certain outcome; contesting the ball is a lottery. Do the math and the foul only pays if the catch was at least 83% likely. Deep balls are caught just 29% of the time. So the foul isn't a bargain — it's insurance you should buy only when you're already beaten and the catch is a near-lock. Grab early on every deep shot and you're lighting points on fire.

The thread

Football's folk wisdom is mostly about looking decisive — not about the math.

01The run doesn't set up the pass. Sequencing is a story we tell; the defense doesn't read it.
02Being predictable isn't the weakness. The best callers commit to the right call and dare you to stop it.
03Icing the kicker is theater. A quarter-century of kicks can't separate it from luck.
04Timeouts are wasted in public. The tape names who burns them and who lets them die.
05The "dumb" penalty can be the rational one — but only in the exact spot instinct already tells a beaten defender to grab.
